author: reek
body: `watch-ports` and `dev` are different things and the names are close enough to be worth separating here. `watch-ports` is the I/O port probe list; `dev` holds the MEMORY watch table from `Dev chapter DevState`, which is what `dbg watch` in the design means.

author: reek
body: `last-address` stays the one home for the cursor and for what `$` reads. The design's `DevState` record also lists a `last-result`; putting one there would have made two fields holding the same number with nothing checking they agree, so DevState carries the watch table and nothing else. That reasoning is written out in the chapter itself.

author: reek
body: `pending` is what lets a command need a SECOND word. The console dispatches one line at a time, so a command that takes an argument has to say it is waiting and the next line has to know it was expected. Before this, `Memory Write` set a status that said "enter address value" and nothing anywhere consumed the next line: it fell through to the address evaluator, moved the cursor, and no write ever happened. The menu offered a command the console could not perform.

author: reek
body: A read acts at the cursor and answers immediately, the way `watch` does, because the cursor is already how every address in this console is chosen -- an expression moves it, and the command acts there. That keeps one idiom instead of two.

author: reek
body: THE DISK CURSOR IS SEPARATE FROM `last-address`, and it has to be. One is an address in the flat physical space and the other is a sector number on a medium; a single cursor meaning both would read the same number two ways depending on which command was asked, which is the kind of thing that is only noticed after it has dumped the wrong thing.

author: reek
body: A FOURTH CURSOR, and the argument is the one the other three made. An address, a sector, an interrupt vector and a CPUID leaf are four different spaces, and a number from any one of them is meaningless in the others; a single cursor would read the same number four ways depending on which command asked. The leaf cursor earns its place the same way the vector cursor did: `$ + 1` steps to the next leaf, which is how anyone enumerates CPUID.

author: reek
body: `macro-running` IS THE WHOLE RECURSION BOUND. A macro body that runs a macro can reach itself, and under no collector and no stack guard that is a hang. `macro.run` is refused outright while this is set, rather than bounded by a depth counter: a flag is checkable by reading it, a depth limit has to be got right and then trusted, and nothing a debugger macro is for needs nesting.

author: reek
body: `macro-name` carries the name from the first prompt to the second, since defining a macro is the one command here that needs two lines of input. It is not a cursor and nothing reads it outside that pair.

author: reek
body: THE TWO SERIAL FLAGS ARE INDEPENDENT, and the design's command table reads as though they are one mode with two positions (`serial.remote` against `serial.local`). They are not, because they govern opposite directions: mirroring is what the console SAYS on COM1 and remote is what it LISTENS to there, and wanting the first without the second is the ordinary case -- watching a console you are driving by keyboard.

author: reek
body: `serial-line` is the PARTIAL line: bytes arrive one poll at a time and a command is not a command until its terminator does.

author: reek
body: These are PURE. `peek-byte` and `poke-byte` carry no effect row, so the whole of the read and the whole of the write are ordinary functions, and the console's use of them can be tested without a machine.

author: reek
body: All four widths on one line, because the menu item promises all four and because the question an operator has at an address is usually "which of these is it" rather than one width chosen in advance.

author: reek
body: A value outside a byte is REFUSED and nothing is written. `poke-byte` would take the low eight bits and the operator would be told a byte had been stored, which is a different byte from the one they typed. The answer names the value it rejected so the refusal is not mistaken for a write that happened to change nothing.

author: reek
body: IT IS NOT, BECAUSE THE CONSOLE ALREADY ANSWERS THE QUESTION. Every address here is chosen by moving the cursor with an expression, and every command acts there; `watch` additionally takes its length from the dump length, so the region it watches is the region `mem` would have shown. Applying the same two rules leaves each command needing exactly ONE argument: a search is a pattern at the cursor, and a compare is the cursor against one other address. The parser was not needed.

author: reek
body: A pattern is refused rather than truncated. An odd number of characters is a typo, not half a byte, and a non-hex character is a typo too; either one silently dropped would search for something the operator did not ask for and report an address they would then trust.

author: reek
body: The window is the dump length, and the answer names the ADDRESS as well as the offset. An offset alone is a number the operator has to add to something, and the thing they would add it to is the cursor they are about to move.

author: reek
body: A compare reports the FIRST difference and both bytes, not a count. A count says two regions differ and leaves the operator to find where; the offset is the thing they were going to look for next.

author: reek
body: The cost is a byte-wise walk of the search window on the FIRST call only. `map1` in `DebuggerState` caches the result, and every caller already consults that field before calling here.

author: reek
body: It is the shape this project keeps meeting. Nothing was ever blank or obviously wrong, so three menu items showed confident numbers and looked like they worked. The address map in `X86_64Boot` is the referee, and it records no faulting vector anywhere.

author: reek
body: THE WATCH LIST HAD NO WAY TO GROW UNTIL `io.watch` LANDED. `watch-ports` was initialised empty and no command anywhere added to it, so the Port I/O view rendered an empty list on every repaint since it was written -- a menu item that drew a heading and nothing under it, which reads as a machine with nothing to say rather than as a view with no input.

author: reek
body: The cap is here rather than in the view because the view is a repaint: every port in this list is read again on every frame, so the list's length is a per-frame I/O cost and not merely storage.
